description:
SHIPPED s473v (2026-09-16), member 3 of perf round 33.  Runtime-only.

=== THE PROFILE (the lever was chosen from it, not guessed) ===
sb-sprof :cpu over the `strcat` bench row (`my $s=''; $s .= 'x' for 1..20e6`),
1956 samples, self time:

    replace                       35.9 %   <- CL's generic sequence function
    %pcl-str-append (self)        19.1 %
    sb-kernel:ub32-bash-copy      14.5 %   <- the move `replace` dispatches to
    length                         8.8 %
    top level form (the loop)      6.9 %
    to-string                      3.6 %
    sb-kernel:%set-fill-pointer    3.2 %
    GENERIC-+ / GENERIC->          1.7 %

HALF THE ROW WAS A `replace` CALL TO MOVE ONE CHARACTER.  Two causes, both in
the same line: a str-buffer is an ADJUSTABLE fill-pointer string, so `replace`
on it cannot take a bash-copy path and its inner accessor is the hairy one;
and `replace` itself is a full call with four keyword arguments to parse.

The growth policy was the round's fourth candidate and is NOT a cost:
%pcl-str-buffer starts at 16 and doubles, so 20 M appends pay ~20
adjust-arrays in total.  Counted, not assumed.

=== THE SHAPE ===
 * %p-str-data â the string twin of %p-vec-data (rule 11: the SAME guard,
   `array-header-p` + not displaced, and the same "or NIL" answer).  A
   non-displaced adjustable string's data vector starts at its index 0, which
   is what lets the caller index it directly.
 * %pcl-str-blit (inline) â copies N characters into that simple string, with
   a ONE-CHARACTER arm that stores the character and calls nothing.  That arm
   is the shape: `$s .= 'x'` is what strcat does and what every template or
   JSON encoder does.
 * %pcl-str-append â `to-string` inlined locally (its fast path is one
   `stringp` test; the full call was 3.6 %), `s` declared `string` so `length`
   stops being a generic-sequence call (8.8 %), and the blit above.  A buffer
   that is not the plain adjustable-character-string shape falls back to the
   old `replace`: same answer, slower, and nothing in this runtime makes one.

=== THE NUMBERS (A/B, one emission, two cores, interleaved best-of-5) ===
BENCH_RT_B = the 2ac855aa runtime; B/A positive = the OLD runtime is slower.
`uptime` 23:58 load 1.20 1.63 2.00.

  bench       perl(s)   pclA(s)   pclB(s)     B/A    A/perl    (was)
  strcat       0.3077    0.2877    0.6434  +123.6%   0.94x    (2.14x)
  textproc     0.4325    1.0980    1.4514   +32.2%   2.54x    -- #1804's
  regexg       0.3635    0.4347    0.7512   +72.8%   1.20x    -- #1804's
  subste       0.0552    0.1852    0.2425   +30.9%   3.35x    -- #1804's
  json-rt      0.8766    1.5809    1.5839    +0.2%   1.80x
  sortnum      0.0243    0.0680    0.0680    -0.0%   control
  feread       0.4787    0.1237    0.1220    -1.4%   control
  feread2      0.4722    0.1264    0.1256    -0.6%   control
  feread3      0.4788    0.1183    0.1211    +2.3%   control

**PCL IS NOW FASTER THAN PERL ON strcat** (0.94x, from 2.14x).  Peak RSS is
flat: 242912 kB new vs 242556 kB base at N = 20 M.

textproc and json-rt did NOT move on this lever (their `.=` is a small share of
rows dominated by the regex engine) â the +32.2 % / +0.2 % above are #1804's,
carried in the same A/B.

=== GUARD ===
Pl/t/raw-verdict-01.t 70 -> 76 rows, beside the S1 str-buffer rows that were
already there.  Six shapes, each probed against perl 5.40.3 first
(scratch/s473v/probe/strbuf2.pl of the s473v worktree): one-char appends across
a growth boundary, multi-char and EMPTY appends interleaved, a NON-base
character (the buffer is a character string, not a base-string), 4-arg substr
into an appended buffer, a buffer used as a REGEX SUBJECT and then grown
(#477's deferred-cut pin), and appending a NUMBER.

INVERSE VERIFICATION: these rows PASS on a `git archive 2ac855aa` extraction,
and that is the correct answer for a pure speed lever â there is no behaviour
to have been wrong.  They are the correctness NET under the shortcut; the A/B
number above is the bar.
subject: A str-buffer `.=` copies through the UNDERLYING simple string, and a one-character append is ONE store, not a `replace` call (strcat +123.6 %, 2.14x perl -> 0.94x)
